relations_to_review.old_text: Even while gaze is held on a stationary target, the eyes move smoothly and irregularly between brief, rapid movements. This smooth motion is called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It changes the image reaching the [**retina**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Understanding its source is therefore part of understanding the visual signals the brain receives. Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) ask whether the motion begins mainly in muscles or in neural commands sent to them.
relations_to_review.prior_evidence: The frontmatter defines the actual smooth movement; eye chapter identifies it before investigating source.

relations_to_review.old_text: Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift. Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them? Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question]

relations_to_review.old_text: The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway]
relations_to_review.prior_evidence: Storage purpose and movement-to-position meaning are taught before the full-model hypothesis.

relations_to_review.old_text: The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. There are two populations, with excitation within each and inhibition between them. Their firing increases for opposite directions of gaze. This supplies the recurrent interaction needed to maintain a range of stored positions.[^p2-network]

relations_to_review.old_text: The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles. The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward. Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types using their eye movement response parameters. Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.[^p2-recordings]

relations_to_review.old_text: The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. The animals first fixated a stationary target and then tracked a moving target. A wire search coil on one eye measured eye position while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement; there were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.[^p2-recordings][^p2-single]
relations_to_review.prior_evidence: Physical motor-cell role is taught before interpreting what57 recorded units measure.

relations_to_review.old_text: At constant rate, the retained intervals are independent. relations_to_review.old_text: The construction starts with a Poisson process at $M$ times the desired rate and retains every $M$th spike. At constant rate, a retained interval is the sum of $M$ independent exponential intervals. Each initial interval has mean $1/(M\lambda)$ and variance $1/(M\lambda)^2$. The retained interval therefore has mean $1/\lambda$, variance $1/(M\lambda^2)$, and CV $1/\sqrt M$. This preserves the mean rate while reducing variability. Its use at changing rates is part of the model; the simple interval derivation assumes a constant rate.
